@@84354922 <h> Why you should be choosing responsibly sourced seafood <p> In Australia , seafood is a way of life . Our coastlines are rich with bait shops and tinnies . Christmas would n't be the same without a plate of fresh prawns . And we 've all spent a hot night in line at the neighbourhood fish-and-chip shop . <p> But we also want to find ways to reduce our global footprint . We 're more considered than ever in the transport we use , the products we buy and the food we eat . The good news is that responsible fish farming is bringing environmentally friendly seafood to our dinner tables , and it 's backed by strict requirements that benefit everyone . <h> Responsible seafood is already available <p> Fish is an ideal food for a burgeoning global population . It 's high in protein , low in fat and full of nutrients . It 's also one of the most efficient converters of feed into high-quality protein , just one of the ways that makes it better bang for your environmental buck than other food sources . <p> Wild caught and farmed seafood are both important @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ stocks are finite . More than 30 per cent of wild fisheries are reported as over fished . Even with sustainable practises , the potential for expansion of wild catch is limited . Responsible aquaculture must fill the gap . <p> Enter : responsible fish farming . And it 's already up and running . Each year , the world produces more farmed fish than it does beef , and more than half the fish consumed worldwide comes from aquaculture . Independent organisation the Aquaculture Stewardship Council ( ASC ) is a global non-profit that ensures fish farms adhere to strict environmental and social welfare conditions and its certification is internationally recognised as ensuring farms meet best practice . They 've done the hard work so all you have to do is look for the green ASC label next time you buy fish . <p> The ASC ensures aquaculture operators adopt practices that are good for the environment and workers , as well as being commercially viable . What 's more , ASC certified farms are independently checked on a regular basis to confirm that they meet the highest environmental @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ by both some of the poorest farmers in developing countries and by multinational companies . <h> Responsible farming considers many factors <p> While aquaculture has many benefits , the rapid rise in demand for farmed fish comes with its own challenges . Issues such as water pollution , disruption to local ecosystems and poor working conditions must be mitigated . <p> Creating sustainable seafood practices is two-fold : it needs to consider both the impact on the environment , and the conditions for producers and their workers . For a business to be truly sustainable , it must adhere to guidelines for fair and equitable workplaces , such as those outlined by the UN Sustainable Development Goals . <p> The ASC 's standards are created through collaboration among multiple stakeholder groups to get the balance right . <p> " Responsible production is not just about protecting the environment , " says Duncan Leadbitter , ASC 's commercial manager for Australia and New Zealand . " Producers need to ensure that workers and communities are treated fairly and equitably . ASC standards cover both these key attributes of responsible production . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ envisages food production that delivers social benefits with minimal environmental impact . Its certification program rewards producers for their good practices and holds them accountable . The label can only be earned , not bought . <p> To become certified , farms , suppliers and products must meet stringent criteria , including only using feed from sustainable sources . To ensure the integrity of the program , farms must be able to demonstrate their eligibility to a certification body that is independent from both the farmer and the ASC . Once certified , they are monitored to ensure they continue to operate in line with requirements . <p> Best practice farms also earn the support of local communities , a concept known as social license . Afterall , the oceans are shared by everybody . <p> This level of independence and transparency is vital to ASC 's goals . All farms carrying ASC certification are listed in detail on the ASC website . Anyone can view information such as who owns them , when they were last audited and , for how long their certification is valid and , most @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Leadbitter explains why certification is so important . " Like any other product , not all farmed seafood is produced responsibly , " he says . " Certification to the ASC standards provides assurance to consumers that ASC-certified seafood is produced responsibly and the supply chain , right to your plate , is secure . " <p> Certification has real impact . We 've all heard that eating red meat contributes towards the production of damaging greenhouse gases . Farmed finfish convert feed into body mass six times more efficiently than cattle and sheep , while producing less than a tenth of the CO2 per kilogram . That means as well as being good for you , switching to fish helps tackle climate change . <p> Economies , and coastal communities , are buoyed by responsible fish farming which provide jobs and opportunities outside of cities . Leadbitter says Australia has the largest number of ASC certified species of any country in the world . <p> " Production is growing rapidly and consumers buy a mix of domestic and imported farmed seafood products , " he says . " There @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Based on its dynamic performance over the last 30 years , it is likely that the future growth of the fisheries sector will come mainly from aquaculture . <h> Look for the labels to make the right choice <p> If you 're looking for sustainable seafood , how do you know what to buy ? <p> The ASC adheres to the highest standard of any organisation , using strict guidelines to ensure its certification is meaningful . It says the use of its logo is a key part of its effort to move the whole industry towards responsibility and sustainability . <p> Products displaying the logo send a strong message about the environmental and social integrity behind them , and take away the guesswork for consumers . When we see the green ASC label on a seafood product , we can be sure it 's traceable back to a responsible farm . <p> Making good choices about the food we eat makes another statement : sustainability matters . We want to eat without hurting the environment . We want to hold producers to high standards . And we know that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ have fish and chips on the beach for years to come . <p> If you choose fish with the ASC logo , you know it can be traced from farm to fork . <p> The Aquaculture Stewardship Council is an independent , international non-profit organisation that manages the world 's leading certification and labelling programme for responsible aquaculture . Look for the green ASC label when purchasing your seafood. 
@@84374313 <h> If and when it has time , the UK must ponder its post-Brexit biotech options <h> Boris Johnson has championed UK bioscience enthusiastically since being elected in December and securing the UK 's withdrawal from the EU . Ben Cooper ponders where the UK might go on GM regulation after the end of the Brexit transition period , and what this may mean for UK-based food manufacturers . <p> In the three years after the UK 's referendum on EU membership , it was often said Brexit had monopolised the political agenda leaving precious little " bandwidth " for anything else . But who would have imagined an issue of such magnitude was about to emerge that would consign Brexit to the " and in other news " section of TV bulletins ? <p> That the biggest Brexit story last week was that EU negotiator Michel Barnier had tested positive for coronavirus and David Frost , his UK counterpart , is self-isolating after showing symptoms , tells its own story . <p> A few critical and challenging issues had dominated the long debates over the UK 's membership of the EU , while undeniably important topics , including @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ biotechnology , were relatively little discussed . However , UK prime minister Boris Johnson is going some way to correcting that . <p> Boris backs British biotech <p> Since securing his premiership and withdrawal from the EU , Johnson has repeatedly made a point of championing deregulation and divergence from the EU on GM as a Brexit boon for the UK and a priority for his administration . Johnson also appointed George Eustice , a longstanding and vocal critic of the EU approach , as Secretary of State at the Department for the Environment , Food and Rural Affairs ( Defra ) . <p> Based rigidly on the precautionary principle , EU regulations both on planting GM crops and commercialising foods made from GMO ingredients are considered by many scientists overly restrictive and lengthy . Over the years , governments and policymakers from across the political divide have sympathised with that view but could do no more than push for reform in Brussels . <p> Johnson now has the opportunity to put the UK on a different footing . His intended direction of travel is clear , though GM is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ instincts . <p> There has been strong support for deregulation on biotech in the scientific community for many years , so Johnson 's remarks have been welcomed enthusiastically by crop scientists . <p> Professor Jonathan Jones of The Sainsbury Laboratory crop research institute , a practitioner and energetic proponent of GM technology for three decades , bemoans the " glacial " progress of GM regulation , but says the Johnson rhetoric is " exciting " . <p> However , he cautions : " Of course , he 's not delivered everything he 's promised in the past but I think he 's serious on this one . How rapidly we get there from here I do n't know . It 's complicated . " <p> Consumer fears easily provoked <p> A prime challenge is the consumer concern and suspicion GM has always attracted . This has engendered a highly cautionary approach by retailers , as reflected in a comment from Andrew Opie , director of food and sustainability at UK food retail trade body The British Retail Consortium , for this article . " Retailers do not currently sell genetically-modified @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ unless there is a change in consumer demand , " Opie says . <h> " Activist groups often behave irresponsibly in terms of inflaming public fears about something that is totally benign " <p> Others would say consumer fears which , while borne partly out of the understandable natural caution people have about technology related to food , are stoked by misinformation and sensationalised reporting , resulting in the retailers ' and public policy being led by the least well informed on the topic . " Activist groups often behave irresponsibly in terms of inflaming public fears about something that is totally benign , " Prof. Jones contends . <p> Food manufacturers have also been somewhat reticent about supporting GM publicly , even if they recognise the benefits of the technology . <p> Asked by just-food for its view on where the UK should go on biotech , the UK food manufacturing representative body The Food and Drink Federation , states : " FDF believes that modern biotechnology , including genetic modification and new breeding techniques , offers considerable potential to improve the quality and quantity of the food supply @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ food using fewer resources and with less impact on the environment . FDF recognises that the impact of biotechnology must be objectively assessed , based on sound science and evidence , and be underpinned by an effective regulatory landscape . " <p> The recognition of the potential benefits but a reluctance to go into battle on behalf of GM can clearly be seen in that statement . While Prof. Jones brands current policies on GM as the " tyranny of the more risk-averse " , he says he " totally understands the brand reputation pressures both manufacturers and retailers are under " . They see " a little bit of upside in terms of cost reduction but a vast amount of downside in terms of risking damage to my precious brand " . <p> All this means biotech has been somewhat friendless , not receiving the widespread support from the private sector that technological innovation in other fields often can . Its backing by " Big Agri " has obviously been significant globally but the associations within that sector help foster some of the distrust , giving environmental campaigners a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ public . <p> Farmer support <p> The National Farmers Union has generally been more publicly supportive of GM , however . Helen Ferrier , chief science and regulatory affairs adviser at the NFU , says it supports a " proportionate and enabling " regulatory framework on GM . <p> Vicki Hird of food and environment pressure group Sustain , however , suggests the picture is more mixed . " There 's a lot of farmers I know who are n't members of the NFU who have a position on GM and biotech which is quite different from the NFU , " Hird says , adding that protection of their European market will be a prime concern for many , underlining the influence ongoing negotiations could have on the UK 's biotech ambitions . <p> " The UK currently remains aligned with the EU in its approach to genetically modified food . The UK 's stance beyond January 2021 will depend very much on the outcome of trade negotiations , " the BRC 's Opie says . <p> Gene-editing move ? <p> Where there could be more immediate progress is in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , director of Cambridge Crop Research , part of the National Institute of Agricultural Botany ( NIAB ) , is leading research utilising modern gene-editing techniques , including CRISPR-Cas9 , to modify the genetic make-up of the Fusarium venenatum fungus , the mycoprotein source for meat substitute brand Quorn , owned by Philippines group Monde Nissin . <p> " We 're trying to understand how the fungus uses different carbon sources , and also how it regulates responses to nitrogen as well , because if we could understand that , then we 'd be able to use a far greater range of crop-based carbon sources to produce mycoprotein , " Harrison explains . <p> Being able to vary what mycoprotein is fed on could broaden the options for how and where mycoprotein can be sustainably produced as a meat alternative . The research is funded by the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council , with Quorn manufacturer Quorn Foods , a subsidiary of Monde Nissin , as a project partner and co-funder . <p> However , Harrison stresses the objective is not to produce a genetically engineered Fusarium venenatum that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ techniques are being used as " a research tool to validate our hypotheses " . <p> Speaking to just-food last year , then Quorn Foods CEO Kevin Brennan said the company would " never go anywhere near genetic modification " . This is not surprising and is common position among food companies . Owing to a 2018 European Court of Justice ruling , any food produced from ingredients derived from the gene-editing processes Harrison 's team is employing would be subject to the EU 's GM regulations and would have to be labelled as containing GMOs . <p> Brennan said the research " provides underpinning science for alternative carbohydrates but also to support feed optimisation " . He continued : " If we can understand at a granular level what the organism reacts to we can optimise feedstock to encourage the ideal growth " . <p> Ironically , some older and less accurate mutagenesis techniques , such as using gamma radiation and chemicals to alter genetic profile , fall outside the EU regulation . " <p> Climate emergency <p> With regard to the regulation of genetic technologies in food production overall , Harrison urges a strictly evidence-led approach , not least given the challenges posed by climate change . <p> " There is enormous potential to grow crops with fewer pesticides by using naturally-occurring , disease-resistance genes . You could do that through traditional breeding but that takes a long time and costs a lot of money . Genetic technology makes it a lot faster and we should really have access in the 21st century to those technologies because we rapidly need to reduce our greenhouse gas emissions . Genetic technology could really be a powerful tool to accelerate our decarbonisation of the foodchain . " <p> While recognising the benefits of separating gene-editing technology from GM , Prof. Jones is concerned arguing in favour of this may unintentionally lend weight to the view that there is still something to be feared in genetic engineering . " There are literally dozens of technologies like that that would be fantastic for the sustainability @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ moving genes from one plant to another or by moving genes between bacteria and plants which is something that 's happened naturally in evolution scores of times , " he says , strongly urging the government to follow through on its supportive stance on GM . <p> Nevertheless , gene editing could be the more immediate move that is easier to negotiate politically and practically . It is also almost impossible to imagine the UK moving out of the transition period with an ECJ ruling featuring in its legislation . Ferrier believes the UK could also work with other member states , many of which were concerned by the ECJ ruling , to move EU opinion on the issue . " This is the opportunity to work with other member states who are similarly concerned about it . That is an area that the UK research sector can have a strength in and it is a really exciting area for developing products that farmers could grow . More than a symbolic event , it unites people together in raising awareness about climate change . <p> However , due to COVID-19 , Earth Hour will be going online with live performances and discussions on how to your part to save the planet . @@84414511 <h> Join in for Earth Hour tonight at 8.30pm <p> Tonight from 8.30-9.30pm it 's Earth Hour , a yearly movement taking place on the last Saturday of March that calls attention to climate change and promote better treatment of our planet . The initiative , which was started by the World Wide Fund for Nature ( WWF ) , took root as a lights-out event in Sydney back in 2007 . Since then however , it has grown into one of the world 's largest grassroots environment-focused movements , with millions of people in over 180 countries now engaging every year . <p> Hongkongers have always shown support for Earth Hour in a big way , like in 2017 , when over 5600 companies and 300 schools took part in the movement , or in 2018 when more than 11,000 city dwellers pledged to turn off non-essential lighting for the event . This year , two of our city 's top restaurants , Amber and Somm , will be observing Earth Hour by replacing all lights in their dining areas with candles between 8-10pm .
